why: One knob moves: 1000 matches to 5000. Everything else is ci-95, which the three-seed loop reproduced to the digit -- seeds 1, 2 and 3 at lambda 0.9 with the ADR 0048 baseline came back 0.6625, 0.0975 and 0.3038 against search-4, a width of 0.565, and 0.7250, 0.7987 and 0.8213 for the clone against Greedy, exactly what ci-88, ci-90 and ci-91 had scored one at a time. So the machinery is trusted and the question is the width. It is variance between fits, from the draw of the dataset alone, and five times the data is the plainest way to shrink it. An expectation written down before the run: if that is what the width is, it should fall by about the square root of five, from 0.565 toward 0.25 on value-vs-search-4. The last expectation written before a run (ci-89) was refused in both directions, so this is a number to check and not a claim. What to read: spread.json, the width column, row by row against ci-95's -- 0.565, 0.121, 0.133 for the value policy against search-4, Greedy and Random, 0.096 and 0.058 for the clone against Greedy and search-4. A narrower spread means the measurement got steadier, not that the policy got better; keep those apart. Expect nothing to be committed: the clone must clear 0.5 against Greedy on every seed AND measurably beat the champion ci-69 on every seed, and at 1000 matches seed 3 lost to it. If every seed beats the champion this time, that is the real thing and worth saying loudly -- and worth checking per seed, not on the mean. The cost is named in the journal: roughly an hour and a half to two hours a turn.
